sections.section_title: The Parable of the Ten Virgins: Preparedness for Delay
sections.summary: Ten virgins await the bridegroom; the five foolish bring lamps but no reserve oil, and when the bridegroom arrives after a long delay their lamps are failing; they cannot borrow oil from the wise, the door shuts behind those who were ready, and the foolish are told 'I do not know you' in language that echoes the exclusion formula of 7:21-23.
sections.relevance: The parable directly presents human preparation as the sole determinant of entry or exclusion from the wedding feast. All ten virgins had lamps, all went out to meet the bridegroom, all slept during the delay — the only difference was what they chose to carry with them, a decision made before the crisis arose. The neutral reading identifies the author's consistent usage of phronimos (wise) and moros (foolish) as distinguishing those who 'hear and act' from those who 'hear and do not act' (7:24-26). The oil — whatever sustains readiness over time — 'cannot be borrowed at the last moment from someone else; each person's readiness is their own.' The concluding imperative 'Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour' addresses the disciples as persons genuinely capable of choosing preparedness or complacency. The 'Lord, Lord' / 'I do not know you' exchange directly echoes 7:21-23, where the criterion for entry was doing the will of the Father — establishing that external identification with Jesus is insufficient without the corresponding inner reality. The parable presents no mechanism by which God determines which virgins are wise and which foolish; the distinction is entirely in their own prior action.
key_phrases: five of them were foolish and five were wise (pente morai kai pente phronimoi)
the foolish took their lamps but took no oil with them
since there will not be enough for us and for you (mepote ou me arkese hemin kai hymin)
those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut
Lord, lord, open to us — I do not know you (ouk oida hymas)
watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour

sections.section_title: The Parable of the Talents: Faithful Use of What Is Entrusted
sections.summary: A master entrusts three servants with talents proportional to their ability before departing on a journey; after a long time he returns to settle accounts, commends the two who doubled their entrustment with identical words ('well done, good and faithful servant — enter into the joy of your master'), and condemns the third who buried his talent out of fear as 'wicked and slothful,' casting him into outer darkness.
sections.relevance: The parable directly conditions the servants' final destiny on their own conduct during the master's absence. The five-talent and two-talent servants receive identical commendation — the neutral reading stresses that 'the absolute amount produced is irrelevant; the faithfulness is what matters' — establishing that God's unequal distribution of capacity does not determine outcomes, since both equally faithful servants receive the same reward. The one-talent servant's condemnation is explicitly for inaction: he 'failed to do anything at all,' and even the most minimal, risk-free action (depositing with bankers) would have sufficed. The master's verdict — poneros kai okneros (wicked and slothful) — is a moral judgment on the servant's choice, not on a predetermined status. The neutral reading emphasizes that this servant 'was not a stranger or an enemy; he was entrusted, known, and given responsibility proportional to his ability,' making his judgment harsher because he had genuine opportunity. The redistribution principle — 'to everyone who has, more will be given; from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away' — governs productive faithfulness: those who use what they are given receive more; those who do not lose even that. The formula 'outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth' consistently applies to insiders who had genuine opportunity but failed to act (8:12, 13:42, 22:13).
key_phrases: to each according to his ability (hekasto kata ten idian dynamin)
well done, good and faithful servant (eu doule agathe kai piste)
you have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much
enter into the joy of your master (eiselthe eis ten charan tou kyriou sou)
you wicked and slothful servant (ponere doule kai oknere)
to everyone who has, more will be given... from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away
cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness

sections.section_title: The Son of Man Judges the Nations: The Criterion of Concrete Mercy
sections.summary: The Son of Man, seated on his glorious throne, gathers all nations and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, inviting the righteous to inherit the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world based on six concrete acts of mercy toward 'the least of these my brothers,' and sending the condemned into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels based on their failure to perform those same acts — with both groups surprised to learn they were serving or failing to serve the King himself.
sections.relevance: This is the document's definitive judgment scene, and the criterion of separation is exclusively human conduct — six concrete acts of mercy (feeding, giving drink, welcoming strangers, clothing, visiting the sick, coming to prisoners). The neutral reading stresses that the righteous 'did not know they were serving the King' — their acts were 'spontaneous responses to need,' not calculated performances — yet those genuine human choices determined their eternal destiny. The condemned are judged for omission: 'they did not actively persecute the hungry or the stranger; they simply did not feed them or welcome them.' The phrase 'kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (v. 34) describes the kingdom's prior existence as an intended destination, not the predetermination of specific individuals; the neutral reading notes it is 'not an improvised reward but a planned inheritance.' The critical asymmetry — the kingdom was prepared 'for you' but the eternal fire was prepared 'for the devil and his angels' — indicates that blessing is the intended destination for humanity, and the fire is entered by those whose conduct aligned them with the devil's program rather than the King's. No mechanism of divine selection determines which side a person stands on; the sole criterion is what each person did or failed to do.
key_phrases: he will separate them one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats
come, you who are blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world
I was hungry and you gave me food... I was in prison and you came to me
as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me
depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels
I was hungry and you gave me no food... you did not visit me
as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me
these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life
